extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, patent prosecutors, in-house counsel, and patent practitioners analyzing Section 101 case law
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and case-derived criteria for evaluating whether patent claims satisfy 35 U.S.C. §101 (are patent-eligible), focusing on whether claims are directed to an abstract idea/natural phenomenon or to a specific technological improvement/inventive concept. Draws on many district and Federal Circuit holdings across software, electrical, mechanical, and biotech fields.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concrete steps beyond abstract thinking
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that include concrete, physical steps requiring more than the abstract thinking capabilities of a person or a computer are less likely to be deemed abstract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E.g., ‘‘Detecting the presence of a person at a door, sending a video of the person to be viewed, and speaking with the person at the door are all concrete steps requiring more than the abstract thinking capabilities of a person or a computer,’’ and thus patent-eligible in that context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recitation of specific technological solutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that recite specific technological solutions (as opposed to mere goals or results) are less likely to be directed to an abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example language: claims reciting ‘‘identifying and refining a conversational flow so that different connection flows can be associated with each other and ultimately an underlying application or protocol’’ were held not directed to an abstract idea because they recited a specific technological solution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific technical solution to a specific technical problem
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim directed to a specific technical solution to a specific technical problem (e.g., transparent data compression for telecommunications) supports patent-eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts look for an identifiable technical problem and a claimed technical solution that addresses it (e.g., ‘‘creating a method for compressing data in a transparent manner’’ was an eligible technical improvement).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tangible, nonabstract device with unconventional component combination
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims focusing on a tangible device whose components are combined in an unconventional way to provide new functionality are less likely to be abstract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Haptic feedback claims were found eligible where they ‘‘focus[ed] on a tangible, nonabstract device . . . which, through the allegedly unconventional combination of components, contain[ed] the new and useful feature of notifying the device’s user of independent events through vibration.’’

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims as improvements to existing technology
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that demonstrate an improvement on existing technology (e.g., reducing hardware, bandwidth, processing needs) indicate patent-eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: eliminating multiple synchronized imaging cameras and minimizing bandwidth/processing needs; improving search speed to allow searching video content ‘‘almost instantaneously.’’ Courts frequently cite concrete technological improvements as dispositive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unconventional arrangement of claim elements (inventive concept)
rubrics_metrics.description: An unconventional arrangement or ordered combination of claim elements can supply the requisite inventive concept under step two (Alice).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts treat the unconventionality of the claimed combination as a factual inquiry: if the ordered combination is ‘‘non-generic and non-conventional’’ in the industry, that supports eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enhancement of conventional systems via specific mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that enhance conventional systems by describing concrete mechanisms (e.g., converting various management data into a common format enabling remote monitoring) are more likely patent-eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The presence of specific conversion/communication mechanisms that enable new functionality (remote monitoring/access) distinguishes claims from abstract ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims not merely stating results but reciting how accomplished
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that do more than state a desired result (i.e., they also recite how that result is accomplished using specific structures or steps) weigh toward eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E.g., displaying location-relevant communications was eligible where the claims recited using location retrieved from a location server and functions stored in a datastore — i.e., how it was done, not only the result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims tied to specific computer architectures or data structures
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitations specifying particular architectures or data-structures (multi-layered data structures, semantic-to-nonsemantic routing) that improve scalability or flexibility indicate a technological improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have held that reciting ‘‘specific attributes’’ such as these can demonstrate the claimed invention is directed to a purported improvement to system flexibility/scalability rather than an abstract idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficient factual development and claim construction required before eligibility determination
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts may deny dismissal when the defendant’s analysis is inadequate or when factual development / claim construction are needed to determine whether claims are abstract or contain an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a defendant provided ‘‘inadequate analysis and explanation of the substance of the claimed inventions, the prosecution history, and potential construction issues’’ so dismissal was denied without prejudice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims that merely state conventional steps/methods without specific means are abstract
rubrics_metrics.description: When claims describe known activities (e.g., sending/receiving/authenticating logon information) with no specific means for improving technology, they are often held abstract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court language: claims ‘‘directed to the abstract idea of ‘sending, receiving, and authenticating logon information, and not to a ‘specific means or method for improving technology.’’’

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims solving problems rooted in computer technology are favorable
rubrics_metrics.description: If the problem is rooted in computer technology (not merely business/abstract problems) and the claim solves that computer-technology problem, courts treat that as evidence of eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E.g., addressing the need for unique installation patches per release channel was characterized as solving a problem rooted in computer technology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims improving computer functioning (efficiency without sacrificing quality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that make the computer ‘‘function’’ better (e.g., more efficient sound processing without quality loss) favor eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts distinguish claims that improve how computers operate from those that merely use computers as tools to perform abstract ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims directed to concrete device features and resource management tied to technology
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims specifying device components configured to perform functions (and addressing problems like battery consumption) are patent-eligible when tied to technological solutions rather than generic resource conservation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a ‘‘recording/play-back apparatus’’ with a controller for monitoring modes and power consumption was eligible where the patent described battery-consumption problems and how the controller improved devices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims that recite particular processing steps tethered to physical inputs/outputs
rubrics_metrics.description: Where claimed processing steps are tied to physical inputs/outputs (e.g., camera images of user’s real physical space mapped into a virtual environment), the claims are less likely abstract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts emphasize that mapping images from a user’s physical location into a virtual environment with specific instructions is not something humans can perform and thus may be patent-eligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims describing novel UI/interaction structures as structural improvements
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that define specific user-interface components or dialog structures that facilitate new presentation/sorting/selection behavior can be patent-eligible as structural improvements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E.g., using a query dialog box designed to permit construction of filters and sort orders on the same screen was treated as a specific structural improvement over general methods of selecting/sorting data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims producing tangible, physical results from sensor inputs
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that recite tangible physical results produced from sensor inputs (e.g., orientation status tracking with six-axis/nine-axis sensors and error correction) are less abstract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts note such claims ‘‘entail more than simply performing a calculation or organizing information through mathematical correlations’’ when they yield tangible effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims directed to concrete physical tasks with specific tangible items in sequence
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that require performing specific physical tasks using specific tangible items in a specific order are not abstractions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: pipe-pulling claims were held ‘‘not drawn to an abstraction, but to a concrete task’’ requiring specific physical tasks and tangible items in a specific order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims that remove prior art dependencies or intermediaries via technical means
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that eliminate previously necessary third parties or intermediaries through a technical mechanism (e.g., transferring bar code data between mismatched systems) support eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts view solutions that remove dependency on ‘‘sophisticated software developed by third parties’’ through claimed mechanisms as technological improvements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims addressing real-world operational problems in prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: When the specification and claims identify concrete prior-art problems (e.g., failures to scan, detect theft) and claim elements address those problems, eligibility is supported.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts rely on allegations that the patented elements ‘‘allege to help resolve such problems’’ as evidence of technological improvement rather than abstract ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims that are improvements in machine/device-read reliability
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that overcome technological limitations of machines (e.g., improving RFID tag readability) are treated as technological inventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The specification’s clear statement that the invention overcomes prior limitations (reader failures vs theft detection) supports eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims that improve industry-specific processes via technology
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that implement technology to improve narrow industry processes (e.g., turbine engine wash quality/safety) support eligibility when they are distinct from prior art methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have found such industry-specific technological improvements ‘‘improve the narrow industry’’ and are not mere abstract ideas executed by a computer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims that are tied to specific packet-level network mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that classify at packet level and optimize data flow by assigning QoS characteristics are treated as technical solutions to technical problems in networking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E.g., ‘‘classifying, on a packet level, what the ideal quality of services characteristics are for each type of data in order to optimize data flow’’ was held to present a technical solution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract idea + specific inventive solution (step two support)
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if a claim is characterized as directed to an abstract idea, it can survive §101 under Alice step two if it contains a specific, inventive solution addressing recognized technical problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: deterministic mass messaging claims were held directed to communicating with groups quickly (abstract), but survive because they ‘‘present[ed] a specific, inventive solution to the problem . . . with messaging networks.’’

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether an ordered combination is conventional is a factual question
rubrics_metrics.description: Determining whether an ordered combination of claim elements is conventional/non-generic is typically a factual determination that can preclude dismissal at pleadings stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts often deny early dismissal where there is insufficient evidence to conclude the combination is conventional; factual development may be required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims framed as improvements to device functioning rather than generic data handling
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts distinguish claims that tie limitations to improved device functioning (e.g., portable device components configured to respond to specific events) from those that generically handle data or use vocabulary to convey information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The presence of ‘‘specific components that are configured to perform specific functions in response to specific events’’ supports eligibility even if some abstract idea is present in part.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims that automate human tasks without inventive concept are abstract
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that simply use computers to perform tasks previously done by humans (without more) are likely directed to abstract ideas lacking inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E.g., claims ‘‘using a computer, instead of human labor, to combine two types of data to form machine code’’ were held abstract with no inventive concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific limiting rules tied to digital image processing may confer eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that require extraction of structural and semantic saliency features and integrating them in particular ways tied to digital image processing can be viewed as technical and unconventional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts consider whether such specific processing steps are ‘‘tied to digital image processing’’ and whether the specification plausibly alleges unconventionality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional improvements in a specific medium can be technological
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying a known method to a particular medium (e.g., linear navigation geared to entertainment in web programs) can be a specific technological improvement if the application produces functional improvements not present in prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ‘‘Present invention improves a specific online search mechanism by creating web programs . . . through ‘linearly linked websites.’’’ Courts may treat novel application to a medium as patent-eligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction and further factual development can affect eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent-eligibility analysis can depend on claim construction and factual development; courts may deny motions where claim construction could change the §101 outcome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: video stream image modification claims where the specification characterized claims as unconventional and further factual development and claim construction could impact eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims relying on specification/expert testimony showing improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim supported by specification statements and expert testimony that the claimed method/framework ‘‘improves on previous data encoding methods’’ can meet the inventive concept requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts give weight to specification characterization and expert testimony at motions stages when evaluating whether the claimed invention confers a technical improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims directed to physical objects readily overcome Section 101 limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims to tangible physical objects (e.g., bedframe, shoes) are generally patent-eligible subject matter under §101.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts state that claims ‘‘directed to a physical object [that] easily overcomes the Section 101 limit on patentability.’’ The specification’s description of manufacturing improvements may further support eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims that improve UI/creation tooling (WYSIWYG) may be technological
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that provide a revolutionary technological solution to create web pages (e.g., WYSIWYG editing engine improvements) have been treated as patent-eligible when they materially improved existing methodologies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court framed web-page creation claims as ‘‘a purportedly revolutionary technological solution to a technological problem’’ and denied dismissal on §101 grounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims that transform natural discoveries into improved processes
rubrics_metrics.description: In biotechnology, claims that apply a natural discovery but then employ it in a new and improved process (with significant practical benefits) can be patent-eligible despite relating to natural phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E.g., cryopreservation claims that ‘‘employed their natural discovery to create a new and improved way of preserving hepatocyte cells for later use’’ were found eligible because the improved process transformed the claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims measuring natural phenomena may be eligible if the measurement method is unconventional
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that measure a natural phenomenon can be patent-eligible if the claimed measurement method is not conventional, routine, or well-understood — i.e., the claim recites unconventional steps or coefficients discovered through development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E.g., a forehead temperature detector claim was held not conventional because the inventor ‘‘determined for the first time the coefficient representing the relationship between temporal-temperature and core body temperature’’ and incorporated that into an unconventional measurement method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims reciting well-known technology performing routine tasks are likely abstract
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that simply combine known technologies to perform routine data processing/storage tasks (e.g., ASR recognizing words and storing fields) without more inventive concept are often held ineligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The automated speech recognition claims were found directed to ‘‘receiving data, recognizing words using well-known ASR technology, and storing the data in the appropriate fields of a report template’’ with no inventive concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims improving navigation/editing workflows can be eligible
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that recite specific methods improving user workflows (e.g., navigating and editing dictation transcripts without stopping playback) can be viewed as improvements in device functionality and thus patent-eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court held transcription error recognition claims eligible because they ‘‘recite[d] specific methods for navigating and editing dictation transcripts more efficiently by eliminating the need to stop the acoustic playback each time a correction is made.’’

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims that secure transactions via anonymous identification can be technological
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims enabling anonymous identification that secures transactions without revealing merchant-identifying information can be considered improvements in computer functionality and thus eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court found such identity-authentication claims ‘‘directed to an improvement in computer functionality by enabling anonymous identification.’’

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims allocating resources in response to received parameters can be inventive
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that receive parameters and allocate resources/data in response may supply an inventive concept if the allocation mechanism is particularized and not generic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: wireless network channel scheduling claims where ‘‘receiving a transmission of such parameters and allocating the data in response to those parameters is an inventive concept.’’

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims to specific software architectures with defined inter-agent features
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that claim a concrete software architecture with facilitators for delegation/coordination, an inter-agent communication language, and a distributed process can be patent-eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court held cooperative software architecture claims not directed to an abstract idea because they recited a ‘‘specific software architecture’’ with enumerated technical features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims addressing content generation/search medium improvements
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that improve the way demand for information is identified, content is generated in response, and how users access information (e.g., pre-indexing in keyword-based engines) are more likely eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts view improvements to search/content delivery mechanisms (pre-indexing, demand identification) as technological improvements rather than abstract ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims to physical transmit/receive devices that improve prior art are eligible
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims reciting physical devices (e.g., wireless transceivers that transmit authorization codes across protocols) that improve prior art device performance are treated as not abstract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court language: claims ‘‘not directed to an abstract idea, but rather to a physical device that improves the prior art.’’
